rejected.title: Punctuation for rhythm and effect
card: Punctuation does more than mark the end of a sentence. Writers choose it on purpose to control how fast a reader moves and where they stress.
Ellipsis
three dots that show a trailing off or a hesitation. "I thought I could... maybe not." The reader slows and hears doubt.
Dash
a sudden break or an added thought. "She opened the door, and there it was: empty." A colon can do a similar job, as it delivers a reveal after a pause.
Short sentence
a very short sentence, even one word, after longer ones. "The rain kept falling through the long, grey afternoon. Silence." It stops the pace and gives the word impact.
rejected.remember: Punctuation sets the pace: dots slow and hesitate, short sentences hit hard.

a.q: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to show hesitation?
opts: "I could tell you the truth... but I'm not sure."
"I could tell you the truth. Never."
"I could tell you the truth: I lied."
"I could tell you the truth, and I will."
a.why: The three dots after truth make the speaker pause and sound unsure. The one-word sentence Never is a blunt stop for impact, not a hesitation.
a.clue: Look for the three dots that trail off.

b.q: A writer ends a long, flowing paragraph about a storm with the one-word sentence "Nothing." What is the main effect?
opts: It halts the pace and gives the word sharp impact
It shows the speaker is hesitating or unsure
It speeds the reader up into the next idea
It adds a second thought to the sentence before
b.why: A very short sentence after long ones breaks the rhythm, so the reader stops and the word lands hard. Hesitation is the effect of an ellipsis, not of a one-word sentence.
b.clue: Think about what a sudden stop does after a long run of words.

version.title: Punctuation for rhythm and effect
card: Writers choose punctuation on purpose. It controls how fast a reader moves through a sentence and which words get the most weight.
Ellipsis
three dots that show a pause, a trailing off or hesitation. In "I think... maybe not", the reader slows down and hears doubt.
Colon
a pause that sets up what comes next. In "She opened the box: empty", the short wait turns the last word into a reveal.
Short sentence
after a run of long sentences, a sentence of a few words, or even one word such as "Silence", stops the pace and makes that word hit hard.
version.remember: Choose punctuation for pace: dots hesitate, a colon sets up a reveal, a short sentence lands hard.

a.q: Which line uses punctuation to show a speaker hesitating?
opts: Well... I suppose I could come along
I know what I need now: a quiet night in
Decided. I am coming along tonight
I could come along, eat, chat and leave
a.why: The ellipsis after Well makes the speaker trail off, so the reader hears doubt. The one-word sentence Decided does the opposite: it sounds firm and certain.
a.clue: Which punctuation mark makes a speaker trail off?

b.q: After a long build-up, Kai ends a mystery scene with "He lifted the lid and saw what was inside: nothing." What is the main effect of the colon?
opts: It makes a pause that sets up the reveal
It shows the speaker trailing off in doubt
It speeds the reader past the word nothing
It joins two items in a list of objects
b.why: The colon makes the reader wait for a moment, so the word nothing lands as a surprise. Trailing off in doubt is the effect of an ellipsis, not a colon.
b.clue: What does a short wait do to the word that comes after it?

a.best: Well... I suppose I could come along

b.best: It makes a pause that sets up the reveal
